title: Reflect[KEY](...) with a const-aliased key is recognized as the panic exit, so the plain return type stands and the function runs
notes: THE ACCEPTANCE HALF of the aliased panic key, and the direction that is easiest to lose without noticing. specification/failures.mdx §Panic Does Not Widen a Return Type (Locked): 'Calling `panic(...)` MUST NOT force a function's return type to widen into `Result<A, Panic>`' and 'A function that validates an argument, refuses a forgery, or asserts an invariant MUST therefore be able to abort with `panic(...)` while keeping a plain return type.' docs/DECISIONS.md carries the matching Locked entry, and both it and failures.mdx:219 add that `Reflect.panic` enters the same distinguished channel. 09-foreign-calls/reflect-panic-under-a-plain-return-type-is-the-same-abort is this program with the member spelled with a dot; the only difference here is a const-aliased element-access key. THE OBSERVABLE THAT MATTERS IS THAT IT COMPILES AT ALL. `guarded` declares `string` and the `if` body returns nothing, so the program type-checks only if the compiler knows that branch ABORTS. Measured on the Go fork before the panic recognizer was routed through the shared member resolution: the aliased key was not recognized as a panic call, the branch looked like an ordinary statement that falls through, and the emitted module was refused by the stock checker with TS2355 — 'a function whose declared type is neither undefined, void, nor any must return a value'. The refusing half of this pair, 09-foreign-calls/an-aliased-reflect-panic-key-is-not-a-value, was a fail-OPEN on the same backend at the same moment. One unrecognized member, two opposite failures, which is why both directions are pinned. `guarded(true)` is called so the panic is never taken: the program runs to completion and prints, which also exercises the lowering rather than only the check.
